source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use a permanent command structure that replaces normal hospital leadership after the incident.","B":"Allow departments to manage the incident independently without shared objectives or resource coordination.","C":"Limit command and coordination to external police, fire, and emergency medical agencies.","D":"Use a standardized scalable structure for command, coordination, resources, and communication during the incident."}}
source_row.rationale: FEMA describes ICS as a standardized, scalable system for command, control, coordination, resources, personnel, facilities, and communication. Option D is correct. It is temporary and incident-focused, promotes coordination rather than independent silos, and is used across sectors including healthcare.
source_row.source_detail: ICS overview: a standardized, on-scene, all-hazards approach to command, control and coordination that integrates facilities, equipment, personnel, procedures and communications within a common organizational structure. Current FEMA NIMS/ICS training content live-rechecked 2026-08-15; NCSBN 2026 Management of Care emergency-response relevance checked. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: prioritization, assignment/delegation, advocacy/client rights, continuity/referral, legal scope, professional limitations and emergency/quality-management activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.
